claim: Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) is arguably the most successful large-scale insect control approach to date.
source: Arguably the most successful large-scale insect control approach to date is Sterile Insect Technique (SIT) (Dyck et al., 2005; Barsanti et al., 1979).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dyck et al., 2005 and Barsanti et al., 1979

claim: SIT uses irradiation at sub-lethal doses to sterilize mass-reared insects prior to their targeted environmental release.
source: SIT uses irradiation at sub-lethal doses to sterilize mass-reared insects prior to their targeted environmental release.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of SIT methodology

claim: SIT was successfully applied to eradicate the New World Screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) from North and Central America over a 50-year period from the mid 1950s to early 2000s.
source: Such an approach was successfully applied to eradicate the New World Screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax) from North and Central America over a 50-year period from the mid 1950s to early 2000s (Scott et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scott et al., 2017

claim: SIT has been successfully applied for the broad-scale control of tephritid fruit flies (e.g. Ceratitis capitata, Zeugodacus cucurbitae, Bactrocera tryoni, and Anastrepha ludens), onion maggots (Delia antiqua), tse-tse flies (Glossina spp.), and several coleoptera and lepidoptera species.
source: SIT has been successfully applied for the broad-scale control of tephritid fruit flies (e.g. Ceratitis capitata, Zeugodacus cucurbitae, Bactrocera tryoni, and Anastrepha ludens), onion maggots (Delia antiqua), tse-tse flies (Glossina spp.), and several coleoptera and lepidoptera species (Dyck et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dyck et al., 2005

claim: Exposing insects to sterilizing doses of irradiation can impact their longevity and mating competitiveness.
source: Exposing insects to sterilizing doses of irradiation can impact their longevity and mating competitiveness (Lance et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lance et al., 2000

claim: Sometimes the lethal dose of radiation is sufficiently close to the sterilizing dose of radiation such that achieving 100% sterilization means that the vast majority of the males will not survive.
source: Sometimes the lethal dose of radiation is sufficiently close to the sterilizing dose of radiation such that achieving 100% sterilization means that the vast majority of the males will not survive (Ricardo Machi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ricardo Machi et al., 2019

claim: Many batch irradiation approaches do not separate males from females prior to release, which can both decrease the effectiveness and lead to public health concerns when the female insect is a disease vector.
source: Many batch irradiation approaches do not separate males from females prior to release, and this can both decrease the effectiveness (Rendón et al., 2004), and lead to public health concerns when the female insect is a disease vector (Benedict, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rendón et al., 2004 and Benedict, 2021

claim: Integrating an early acting female lethality system to New World Screwworm without impacting male fitness and fecundity has the potential to improve SIT effectiveness by several fold.
source: Integrating an early acting female lethality system to New World Screwworm without impacting male fitness and fecundity has the potential to improve SIT effectiveness by several fold (Concha et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Concha et al., 2020

claim: Release of insects with dominant lethality (RIDL) has been successfully demonstrated to suppress target mosquito populations in field trials in the Caribbean islands and South America.
source: Release of insects with dominant lethality (RIDL), has been successfully demonstrated to suppress target mosquito populations in field trials in the Caribbean islands and South America (Harris et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harris et al., 2012

claim: Precision-guided SIT (pgSIT) utilizes expression of Cas9 nuclease to knock out female survival and male fertility genes prior to generate potential biocontrol agents.
source: Precision-guided SIT (pgSIT) utilizes expression of Cas9 nuclease to knock out female survival and male fertility genes prior to generate potential biocontrol agents (Li et al., 2021; Kandul et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2021 and Kandul et al., 2019

claim: Engineered Genetic Incompatibility (EGI) is a strategy for creating bi-directional (male-to-female and female-to-male) mating incompatibility that mirrors the behavior of post-zygotic speciation mechanisms.
source: Engineered Genetic Incompatibility (EGI) is a strategy for creating bi-directional (male-to-female and female-to-male) mating incompatibility that mirrors the behavior of post-zygotic speciation mechanisms. (Maselko et al., 2020; Maselko et al., 2017; Buchman et al., 2021; Waters et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maselko et al., 2020; Maselko et al., 2017; Buchman et al., 2021; Waters et al., 2018

claim: EGI lines are created by engineering flies to express a dCas9-based programmable transcription activator (PTA) that targets the promoter of a gene which is lethal when expressed too high or in the wrong tissues.
source: We created EGI lines by engineering flies to express a dCas9-based programmable transcription activator (PTA) that targets the promoter of a gene which is lethal with expressed too high or in the tissues.
evidence: Describes the methodology used by the authors to create EGI lines

claim: The EGI line is made homozygous for a mutation that prevents binding of the PTA to avoid lethal over- or ectopic-expression.
source: This lethal over- or ectopic-expression is avoided in the EGI line by making it homozygous for a mutation that prevents binding of the PTA.
evidence: Describes the genetic design of the EGI line

claim: The EGI line is true-breeding and has normal fecundity because it is homozygous for both the PTA and the promoter resistance mutation.
source: Because the EGI line is homozygous for both the PTA and the promoter resistance mutation, it is true-breeding and has normal fecundity.
evidence: Describes the phenotypic behavior of the EGI line based on its genetic design

claim: Outcrossing EGI with wild-type produces hybrid offspring that inherit one copy of the PTA and only one copy of the resistance allele, resulting in all hybrid offspring being inviable.
source: However, outcrossing with wild-type produces hybrid offspring that inherit one copy of the PTA and only one copy of the resistance allele. Because the PTA is haplosufficient for lethality (i.e. one copy is lethal) and the resistance allele is haploinsufficient (i.e. strains must be homozygous for the resistance allele to survive in the pressence of the PTA), all hybrid offspring are inviable.
evidence: Describes the genetic mechanism and outcome of EGI x wild-type crosses

claim: Multiple mutually incompatible EGI lines can be created that are incompatible with wild-type and with each other, providing a way to rationally engineer negatively correlated cross-resistance for the first time.
source: Importantly, multiple mutually incompatible EGI lines can be created that are incompatible with wild-type and with each other, providing a way to rationally engineer negatively correlated cross-resistance for the first time (Maselko et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maselko et al., 2020

claim: EGI could be used as a threshold-dependent gene drive.
source: As with other underdominant biocontrol methods, EGI could be used as a threshold-dependent gene drive (Magori and Gould, 2006; Davis et al., 2001; Buchman et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Magori and Gould, 2006; Davis et al., 2001; Buchman et al., 2021

claim: EGI could be coupled to a conditional female-lethal construct to produce a strain that more closely replicates SIT biocontrol agents.
source: Alternatively, it could be coupled to a conditional female-lethal construct, such as the tetracycline (Tet)-repressible positive feedback circuit (Fu et al., 2007; Li et al., 2014), to produce a strain that more closely replicates SIT biocontrol agents.
evidence: Supported by citations to Fu et al., 2007 and Li et al., 2014

claim: The authors successfully engineered a SSIMS system in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Here, we demonstrate the successful engineering of such a system in Drosophila melanogaster.
evidence: This is the main claim of the study, supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: The SSIMS line contains two female lethal (FL) constructs on the X chromosome and an EGI construct on the third chromosome.
source: To generate the SSIMS line, we made a stock that contains two female lethal (FL) constructs (Das et al., 2020) on the X chromosome and an EGI construct on the third chromosome (Figure 1).
evidence: Describes the genetic composition of the SSIMS line, supported by citation to Das et al., 2020 and Figure 1

claim: The female lethal construct contains 21 copies of the tet operator upstream of the Hsp70 promoter.
source: The female lethal construct contains 21 copies of the tet operator upstream of the Hsp70 promoter (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Describes the genetic design of the female lethal construct, supported by citation to Li et al., 2014

claim: An intron from the C. hominivorax tra gene that exhibits sex-specific splicing is present immediately downstream of the start codon and upstream of a coding DNA sequence for the tet transactivator protein.
source: An intron from the C. hominivorax tra gene that exhibits sex-specific splicing (alternative 5' splice sites) is present immediately downstream of the start codon and upstream of a coding DNA sequence for the tet transactivator protein (Figure 1c).
evidence: Describes the genetic design of the female lethal construct, with reference to Figure 1c

claim: In females, the female lethal construct is expected to produce the tTA transgene, while the alternative splicing in males is expected to produce mature mRNA with several stop codons upstream of the tTA CDS.
source: In females, this construct is expected to produce the tTA transgene, while the alternative splicing in males is expected to produce mature mRNA with several stop codons upstream of the tTA CDS.
evidence: Describes the expected behavior of the female lethal construct based on sex-specific splicing

claim: The two-copy strains of the female lethal construct showed a stronger female lethal phenotype compared to one-copy strains.
source: In comparing the behavior of strains containing one- or two-copies of this construct on the X chromosome, the two-copy strains showed a stronger female lethal phenotype, so we used a two-copy strain to construct SSIMS flies (Das et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Das et al., 2020

claim: The EGI construct comprised a dCas9-VPR programmable transcriptional activator (PTA) targeting the promoter of a critical developmental morphogen gene.
source: The EGI construct comprised a dCas9-VPR programmable transcriptional activator (PTA) targeting the promoter of a critical developmental morphogen gene (Figure 1d).
evidence: Describes the genetic design of the EGI construct, with reference to Figure 1d

claim: The study uses a previously described EGI genotype that leverages lethal ectopic expression of the pyramus gene for hybrid incompatibility.
source: In this study, we use a previously described EGI genotype that leverages lethal ectopic expression of the pyramus gene for hybrid incompatibility, but other genotypes are expected to work equally well.
evidence: Describes the specific EGI genotype used in the study

claim: A mutation in the promoter of the pyramus gene was maintained throughout the strain-construction process to prevent binding of the PTA to the pyramus promoter and therefore lethal ectopic expression.
source: Throughout the strain-construction process, a mutation in the promoter of the pyramus gene was maintained to prevent binding of the PTA to the pyramus promoter, and therefore lethal ectopic expression (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Describes the genetic design strategy, with reference to Appendix 1—figure 1

claim: The SSIMS line used the foxo promoter to drive the PTA, as this genotype provided strong genetic incompatibility in previous studies.
source: The SSIMS line used the foxo promoter to drive the PTA, as this genotype provided strong genetic incompatibility in previous studies (Maselko et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maselko et al., 2020

claim: Viable SSIMS flies were generated that contained both visual markers of the FL genotype (GFP expression) and the EGI genotype (red eyes).
source: Following the mating scheme outlined in Supplementary Note 1, we were able to generate viable SSIMS flies, which contained both of the visual markers of the FL genotype (GFP expression) and the EGI genotype (red eyes) (Figure 2a).
evidence: Describes the successful generation of SSIMS flies with visual confirmation, supported by Figure 2a

claim: Other EGI genetic designs or FL designs are predicted to work equally well for engineering SSIMS.
source: Other EGI genetic designs (Maselko et al., 2020; Buchman et al., 2021) or FL designs (Yan and Scott, 2015) are predicted to work equally well for engineering SSIMS.
evidence: Supported by citations to Maselko et al., 2020; Buchman et al., 2021; and Yan and Scott, 2015

claim: The SSIMS line bred true in the presence of Tet at 100 μg/ml and contained both visual markers for FL (GFP) and EGI (mini-white).
source: We confirmed that the SSIMS line bred true in the presence of Tet at 100 μg/ml and contained both visual markers for FL (GFP) and EGI (mini-white) (Figure 2a).
evidence: Experimental validation of SSIMS line behavior, supported by Figure 2a

claim: In the presence of Tet at 10 μg/ml, the SSIMS line shows a slight sex-ratio bias with fewer females (40% female) surviving to adulthood than expected 50%.
source: In the presence of Tet at (10 μg/ml) the SSIMS line shows a slight sex-ratio bias with fewer females (40% female) surviving to adulthood than expected 50% (Figure 2b).
evidence: Experimental data showing sex-ratio bias, supported by Figure 2b

claim: The FL transgene is partially leaky in females at 10 μg/ml Tet.
source: This suggests that the FL transgene is partially leaky in females at 10 μg/ml Tet.
evidence: Inference based on the observed sex-ratio bias

claim: In the absence of Tet, no females survive to adulthood and either die as larvae or pupae.
source: In the absence of Tet no females survive to adulthood and either die as larvae or pupae (Figure 2b).
evidence: Experimental data showing complete female lethality without Tet, supported by Figure 2b

claim: The phenotype of the SSIMS line suggests that sex-specific splicing occurs as previously reported for this genetic construct.
source: While we did not empirically characterize sex-specific splicing, the phenotype of the SSIMS line suggests that sex-specific splicing occurs as previously reported for this genetic construct (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference based on phenotypic data, supported by citation to Li et al., 2014

claim: Wild-type females did not produce any viable adults when mated with SSIMS males.
source: Wild-type females did not produce any viable adults when mated with SSIMS male (Figure 2c).
evidence: Experimental data demonstrating EGI functionality, supported by Figure 2c

claim: There was no difference in fecundity of the wild-type and SSIMS strains when mated to their own type in a head-to-head comparison.
source: There was no difference in fecundity of the wild-type and SSIMS strains, when mated to their own type, in a head-to-head comparison (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Experimental data comparing fecundity, supported by Appendix 1—figure 2

claim: In the presence of Tet at concentrations between 10 and 100 μg/ml, there is a consistent but slight sex-ratio bias with 40–45% female offspring.
source: In the presence of Tet at concentrations between 10 and 100 μg/ml there is a consistent but slight sex-ratio bias with 40–45% female offspring (Figure 2d).
evidence: Experimental data showing sex-ratio bias across Tet concentrations, supported by Figure 2d

claim: There is no statistically significant difference in the sex-ratio of offspring across Tet concentrations between 10 and 100 μg/ml.
source: There is no statistically significant difference in the sex-ratio of offspring across these concentrations.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: When offspring raised on Tet are transferred to food without Tet, the number of females that survive in the next generation varies from 0% to 35% in a dose-dependent manner.
source: When these offspring are transferred to food without Tet, the number of females that survive in the next generation varies from 0% to 35% in a dose-dependent manner (R2 = 0.86 to best-fit Hill function, t-value = 24.3, p < 0.00001).
evidence: Experimental data with statistical analysis showing dose-dependent relationship

claim: Parents raised on 10 μg/ml Tet had no surviving female offspring when transferred to Tet-free medium.
source: Parents raised on 10 μg/ml had no surviving female offspring when transferred to Tet-free medium, but parents raised on 100 μg/ml had 35% female offspring on Tet-free medium (Figure 2e).
evidence: Experimental data showing differential female survival based on parental Tet exposure, supported by Figure 2e

claim: Parents raised on 100 μg/ml Tet had 35% female offspring on Tet-free medium.
source: Parents raised on 10 μg/ml had no surviving female offspring when transferred to Tet-free medium, but parents raised on 100 μg/ml had 35% female offspring on Tet-free medium (Figure 2e).
evidence: Experimental data showing differential female survival based on parental Tet exposure, supported by Figure 2e

claim: The delayed female lethality likely arises from maternal deposition of Tet and not genetic instability of the female lethal construct.
source: We confirmed that this likely arises from maternal deposition of Tet and not genetic instability of the female lethal construct by rearing these flies for one additional generation in Tet-free medium.
evidence: Inference based on additional experimental data

claim: 100% female lethality was observed in the second generation of rearing on Tet-free media.
source: We observed 100% female lethality in the second generation of rearing on Tet-free media (Figure 2f).
evidence: Experimental data confirming complete female lethality after maternal Tet is depleted, supported by Figure 2f

claim: In control experiments lacking the SSIMS male, wild-type females had an average of 76 offspring surviving to adulthood.
source: In control experiments lacking the SSIMS male, the females had an average of 76 offspring surviving to adulthood.
evidence: Experimental data from control group

claim: In competitive experiments with one SSIMS male, one wild-type male, and one virgin female, there was a clear bimodal distribution with nine females producing an average of 82 offspring and fifteen females producing zero adult offspring.
source: In the competitive experiments, there was a clear bimodal distribution. Nine females produced an average of 82 females for one mode, and fifteen females produced zero adult offspring.
evidence: Experimental data from male competition assay

claim: Females that produced zero adult offspring in the competition assay had clearly mated, because the females laid eggs that hatched into larva that died soon after.
source: This latter group had clearly mated, because the females laid eggs that hatched into larva that died soon after.
evidence: Observational data confirming mating occurred

claim: Two females produced an intermediate number of offspring, suggesting they may have mated with both wild-type and SSIMS males.
source: There were two females that produced an intermediate number of offspring, suggesting they may have mated with with both wild-type and SSIMS males.
evidence: Inference based on intermediate offspring counts

claim: Fewer offspring survive when SSIMS males are included in the mating vials, and this cannot be explained by the decrease in the number of males that could sire surviving offspring.
source: Fewer offspring survive when SSIMS males are included in the mating vials (Figure 3b), and this cannot be explained by the decrease in the number of males that could sire surviving offspring (p < 0.05 for each comparison).
evidence: Experimental data with statistical analysis, supported by Figure 3b

claim: In Drosophila spp., females can store the sperm from multiple males in their spermathecae which allows for sperm to compete to fertilize the eggs.
source: In Drosophila spp., females can store the sperm from multiple males in their spermathecae which allows for sperm to compete to fertilize the eggs.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about Drosophila reproductive biology

claim: Non-virgin wild-type females with either no males or with wild-type males for re-mating produced an average of 70–90 offspring that survived to adulthood from each vial.
source: Non-virgin wild-type females with either no males or with wild-type males for re-mating, produced an average of 70–90 offspring that survived to adulthood from each vial.
evidence: Experimental data from sperm displacement assay control groups

claim: When SSIMS males were available for re-mating, the number of surviving offspring dropped by 36% within the first egg lay period, and by 98–99% for the next two egg laying periods.
source: When SSIMS males were available for re-mating, the number of surviving offspring dropped by 36% within the first egg lay period, and by 98–99% for the next two egg laying periods (Figure 3c).
evidence: Experimental data from sperm displacement assay, supported by Figure 3c

claim: In the presence of SSIMS males, post-zygotic lethality of eggs and larvae was observed during all three egg-laying periods, which suggests that SSIMS males mated with the females to replace wild-type sperm with SSIMS sperm in the spermathecae.
source: In the presence of SSIMS males, we observed post-zygotic lethality of eggs and larvae during all three egg-laying periods, which suggests that SSIMS males mated with the females to replace wild-type sperm with SSIMS sperm in the spermathecae.
evidence: Inference based on observational data from sperm displacement assay

claim: In both offensive and defensive sperm displacement assays, the average number of surviving offspring following the second mating event decreased to one third the level of the control experiment.
source: In both cases, the average number of surviving offspring following the second mating event decreased to one third the level of the control experiment (Figure 3d).
evidence: Experimental data from offensive and defensive sperm displacement assays, supported by Figure 3d

claim: There was not a significant difference in the number of offspring in offensive or defensive matings.
source: There was not a significant difference in the number of offspring in offensive or defensive matings.
evidence: Statistical analysis of experimental data

claim: Wild-type D. melanogaster will re-mate with SSIMS males in laboratory settings.
source: This demonstrates that wild-type D. melanogaster will re-mate with SSIMS males in laboratory settings, and that the sperm from SSIMS males is competitive for fertilizing female eggs even in the presence of sperm from wild-type males in the spermathecae.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: The sperm from SSIMS males is competitive for fertilizing female eggs even in the presence of sperm from wild-type males in the spermathecae.
source: This demonstrates that wild-type D. melanogaster will re-mate with SSIMS males in laboratory settings, and that the sperm from SSIMS males is competitive for fertilizing female eggs even in the presence of sperm from wild-type males in the spermathecae.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental data

claim: In cages, adults were sustained by feeding a liquid solution of 5% yeast extract and 5% sucrose solution via a cotton wick.
source: In cages, adults were sustained by feeding a liquid solution of 5% yeast extract and 5% sucrose solution via a cotton wick.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: This method of feeding adults was used to overcome the problem of adults getting stuck in semi-solid food containers.
source: This method of feeding adults was used to overcome the problem of adults getting stuck in semi-solid food containers.
evidence: Explanation of methodological choice

claim: A 250-ml bottle (reproduction bottle) with 30-ml standard cornmeal food was introduced to each cage once a week for 24 hr to allow the population to expand.
source: To allow the population to expand, a 250-ml bottle (reproduction bottle) with 30-ml standard cornmeal food was introduced to each cage once a week for 24 hr.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Reproduction bottles were uncapped 10 days after egg-laying and left open for 3 days to allow for the next generation to eclose and integrate with the multi-generational caged population.
source: Reproduction bottles were uncapped 10 days after egg-laying and left open for 3 days to allow for the next generation to eclose and integrate with the multi-generational caged population.

claim: 600 SSIMS flies were released to the two experimental cages at the start of the experiment and for each of the first 8 weeks.
source: At the start of the experiment and for each of the first 8 weeks, we released 600 SSIMS flies to the two experimental cages (approximately 45:55 female:male ratio).
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: The released SSIMS flies had been reared on 100 μg/ml Tet, so the female lethality phenotype from conspecific matings was expected to be delayed by one generation.
source: The released SSIMS flies had been reared on 100 μg/ml Tet, so we expected the female lethality phenotype from conspecific matings to be delayed by one generation (Figure 2d–f).
evidence: Inference based on previous experimental results shown in Figure 2d–f

claim: The SSIMS-treatment cages saw an immediate reduction of fecundity in wild-type females.
source: The SSIMS-treatment cages saw an immediate reduction of fecundity in wild-type females.
evidence: Experimental observation from cage trial

claim: Female fecundity did not follow a normal distribution, but rather was multimodal with a mode at 0 and another mode at about 50, likely representing females that had mated with SSIMS or wild-type males, respectively.
source: Female fecundity did not follow a normal distribution, but rather was multimodal with a mode at 0 and another mode at about 50, likely representing females that had mated with SSIMS or wild-type males, respectively (Figure 4b).
evidence: Experimental data with interpretation, supported by Figure 4b

claim: By week 7, none of the captured wild-type females were fecund.
source: By week 7, none of the captured wild-type females were fecund.

claim: In the control cages, counts of wild-type flies reached a steady-state of approximately 500 flies captured per week.
source: In the control cages (blue lines), counts of wild-type flies reached a steady-state of approximately 500 flies captured per week (Figure 4c).

claim: The total cage population was estimated by visual inspection to be approximately three times larger than the number of trapped/counted flies.
source: While cages were too large to allow for counting of all of the individuals, we estimate by visual inspection that the total cage population was approximately three times larger than the number of trapped/counted flies.

claim: In the SSIMS treatment cages, the counts of wild-type flies dropped continuously throughout the experiment.
source: In the SSIMS treatment cages, the counts of wild-type flies dropped continuously throughout the experiment.

claim: By week 10, there were no wild-type females identified in the weekly traps.
source: By week 10, there were no wild-type females identified in the weekly traps.

claim: The number of SSIMS flies, both males and females, remained high in the trap counts during weeks 1 to 8 when weekly releases occurred.
source: The number of SSIMS flies, both males and females, remained high in the trap counts during weeks 1 to 8 when weekly releases occurred.

source: Male SSIMS flies disappeared from the cages a few weeks later.

source: To investigate how SSIMS compares to other genetic biocontrol technologies, we developed an agent-based model for Spotted Wing Drosophila (SWD), an agricultural pest that is the target of genetic biocontrol research and development projects (Asplen et al., 2015; Schetelig et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Asplen et al., 2015 and Schetelig et al., 2021

claim: FL and SSIMS generally outperform RIDL by providing more population suppression for the same number of release agents.
source: First, FL and SSIMS generally outperform RIDL by providing more population suppression for the same number of release agents.

claim: FL outperformed double-amplification SSIMS (100 mg/ml Tet) and single-amplification SSIMS (10 mg/ml Tet) at the lowest release numbers.
source: FL outperformed double-amplification SSIMS (100 mg/ml Tet) and single-amplification SSIMS (10 mg/ml Tet) at the lowest release numbers.

source: This is due to the persistence of the FL genotype in the simulated population, even many generations after release.

claim: At moderate release numbers, SSIMS outperformed FL.
source: However, at moderate release numbers SSIMS outperformed FL.

source: The largest advantage of SSIMS over FL comes when analyzing the time to eradication (Figure 5f), where SSIMS achieves population suppression faster than FL.

source: Both single- and double-amplification SSIMS eradicated the wild-type population by the end of June.

claim: SSIMS represents one of the most complex engineered systems demonstrated in insects.
source: This makes SSIMS one of the most complex engineered systems demonstrated in insects.
